topic.subject: maths
topic.examWeightHint: M8 Paper 1 (non-calculator), early to middle of the paper, almost every series. Short Write down the value of parts at a mark each (Summer 2025 Q8: a zero index, minus one and minus three; Summer 2026 Q6: 2^(-2); November 2023 Q10(b): 4^(3/2)), a two-mark show-that for a negative fractional index (November 2025 Q11(b)), and simplifications with negative indices (Summer 2024 Q10). An index equation has also appeared (November 2021 Q11).
mustMemorise: a^(1/n) is the nth root of a, because n copies of it multiply to give a^1
a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)^m: the bottom number is the root, the top number is the power
Take the root first, then the power, so the arithmetic stays small enough for a non-calculator paper
a^(-n) = 1 over a^n, from a^n x a^(-n) = a^0 = 1; the answer is never negative when the base is positive
(a/b)^(-n) = (b/a)^n: a negative index turns a fraction upside down
notOnThisSpec: Logarithms, which appear in no CCEA GCSE Mathematics statement, so a^x = b is never solved that way
Fractional indices whose root is not exact: Paper 1 answers must be exact, so the bases chosen always have whole-number roots
Surd manipulation for its own sake, which belongs to M8-NA-01 and is a separate topic here

Evaluate a negative fractional index by writing the reciprocal line first, then the root, then the power
Apply a negative index to a fractional base by turning the fraction over and making the index positive
Give an exact answer as an integer or a fraction in its lowest terms, because Paper 1 allows no calculator
Reach a printed result in a show-that index question by a written chain of steps
Compare two index values without evaluating them as decimals, using the size of the denominators

sheet.howExamined: M8 Paper 1 only for the exact-value work (non-calculator, 1 hour 15 minutes, 50 marks; the formula sheet on page 2 carries no index law). Expect it early to middle: a three-part question worth 1 mark per part worded Write down the value of, and a two-mark Show that index proof. A single simplification for 3 marks also appears. Schemes award A1 per short value with no working demanded, and M1 A1 on the longer items, where the method mark is for the root or the reciprocal being seen and the accuracy mark for the exact value.

Swapping the two numbers of a fractional index, so the denominator becomes the power
Treating a fractional index as a multiplier, so 16^(3/4) becomes 12

noteBlocks.lede: A power began as a count: $2^{5}$ is five twos multiplied. That reading has nothing to say about $2^{-3}$ or $16^{\frac{1}{2}}$, so the meaning is widened in the one way that keeps the index laws true: a negative index is a reciprocal, and a fractional index is a root.
can: Write a zero or negative index as a value without pausing: 1, or one over the power.
Take the root named by the bottom number, then the power named by the top.
Do the three jobs of a negative fractional index in order, fraction bases included.

noteBlocks.md: Walk down the powers of any number and each step divides by that number. The pattern does not stop when the index reaches 0: it gives 1 there, and then one over the power, which is the reciprocal. A negative index never makes the answer negative; it turns the power upside down.

noteBlocks.title: Why the answer stays positive
noteBlocks.md: A positive base raised to any power is positive, so one over it is positive too. The minus sign in the index decides whether the value is above 1 or below it, never its sign.

steps.decision: Each step down divides by 6, and 6 divided by 6 is 1.
The pattern carries on past zero.
It lands on one over $6^{2}$: the reciprocal, still positive.

noteBlocks.explain: $7^{-2}$ is one over $7^{2}$, so it is $\tfrac{1}{49}$. A negative index gives a reciprocal, never a negative number.

twin.explain: $2^{6} = 64$, and the minus sign turns it over: $2^{-6} = \tfrac{1}{64}$.

optionNotes.why: The index is negative, not the answer: $2^{-6}$ is one over 64.
The index was used as a multiplier, $2 \times (-6)$, instead of a power.
Without its minus sign the index gives 64; the minus turns it over.
The minus sign in the index does not make the answer negative; it turns $7^{2}$ over, giving a reciprocal.
A negative index is not a multiplier: $7 \times (-2)$ is not a power of 7.
The minus sign has been dropped: $7^{2}$ is 49, and $7^{-2}$ is its reciprocal.

noteBlocks.text: Why zero gives 1 and minus a reciprocal

noteBlocks.md: The index laws were built for positive powers: multiplying adds the indices, dividing subtracts them. Insist that they keep working and the meaning of a zero or negative index is forced, with no choice left. The same division, done two ways, gives $a^{0} = 1$; a product that comes to $a^{0}$ gives the reciprocal. The argument is short enough to rebuild in the exam if the rule ever slips your mind.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that $a^{0} = 1$ and $a^{-2} = \dfrac{1}{a^{2}}$, for any non-zero $a$.

steps.decision: Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the indices.
Anything non-zero divided by itself is 1, and both lines describe the same division.
Multiplying adds the indices, and the sum is zero.
Two numbers that multiply to 1 are reciprocals. The same argument works for any power: $a^{-n} = \dfrac{1}{a^{n}}$.

noteBlocks.text: A zero index sits on one base

noteBlocks.md: A zero index belongs to the number it sits on and nothing else. In $3 \times 5^{0}$ only the 5 is raised to the power 0, so the 3 in front survives. The two slips to avoid are reading $5^{0}$ as 5 or as 0: it is always 1. So $4^{0} + 4^{0}$ is 2, not 0 and not 8.

noteBlocks.text: Why half a power is a square root

noteBlocks.md: Ask the same question of a fraction: what must $a^{\frac{1}{2}}$ be for the laws to stay true? Two copies multiply to $a^{\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}} = a^{1}$, so it is the number that squares to $a$. In the same way $a^{\frac{1}{3}}$ is the cube root, and the bottom number always names the root. A top number bigger than 1 then says how many of those roots to multiply.

The square root is 8, but the top number 3 still asks for the cube.

The index was used as a multiplier, $100 \times \tfrac{3}{2}$; it asks for a square root and then a cube.
That is the square root only; the top number 3 still asks for the cube.

noteBlocks.text: A negative fraction index: three jobs

noteBlocks.md: A negative fractional index carries three instructions. The minus sign turns the power over; the bottom number is the root; the top number is the power. Do them one line at a time: the reciprocal first, so the minus cannot come back as a minus in the answer. Leaving $3^{-4}$ or a decimal loses the last mark: the question wants the exact fraction.

noteBlocks.text: A fraction base turns upside down

noteBlocks.md: When the base is a fraction, the minus sign is easier still: $\left(\dfrac{a}{b}\right)^{-n} = \left(\dfrac{b}{a}\right)^{n}$. Turn the fraction over and the index becomes positive. Then root the top and the bottom separately, and raise both to the power. The answer is often a fraction bigger than 1, which is the sign that the fraction was turned over.

Which number squares to 169?

commonErrors.feedback: An index of a half is a square root, not a multiplier: $\sqrt{169} = 13$.

parts.stem:
Find the value of $n$ when $8^{n} = \dfrac{1}{32}$.

Give your answer as a fraction.
hints: Write 8 and 32 as powers of the same number.
With the same base on both sides, the indices are equal.

commonErrors.feedback: $\dfrac{1}{32}$ is $2^{-5}$, not $2^{5}$: the reciprocal carries the minus sign into the index.
8 and 2 are different bases, so $8^{n}$ cannot be compared with $2^{-5}$ directly; write 8 as $2^{3}$ first.

emphasis: negative fractional index on a fraction

parts.stem: Work out the value of $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} + 7^{0}$.
hints: A negative index turns a fraction base over.
$4^{\frac{3}{2}}$: square root, then cube.
Any non-zero number to the power 0 is 1.
parts.workedSolution: Turning the fraction over, $\left(\dfrac{1}{4}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}} = 4^{\frac{3}{2}}$. Then $\sqrt{4} = 2$ and $2^{3} = 8$. With $7^{0} = 1$, the value is $8 + 1 = 9$.

commonErrors.feedback: $\left(\tfrac{1}{4}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}} = \tfrac{1}{8}$ ignores the minus sign, which turns the fraction over to give 8.
The power is right; $7^{0}$ is 1, not 0.
The power is right; $7^{0}$ is 1, not 7.
A negative index turns the fraction over; it does not make the value negative.

emphasis: negative fractional index on a fraction

parts.stem: Work out the value of $49^{\frac{3}{2}}$.
hints: The bottom number is 2: a square root.
Then the top number 3: a cube.

commonErrors.feedback: The square root is right; the top number 3 still asks for the cube.
An index is not a multiplier: root, then power.

parts.stem:
Work out the value of $\left(\dfrac{9}{25}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}}$.

Give your answer as a fraction in its lowest terms.
hints: The minus sign turns the fraction over.
Square-root the top and the bottom.
Then cube both.
parts.workedSolution: Turning it over, $\left(\dfrac{9}{25}\right)^{-\frac{3}{2}}$ becomes $\left(\dfrac{25}{9}\right)^{\frac{3}{2}}$. The square root is $\dfrac{5}{3}$, and cubing gives $\dfrac{125}{27}$.

commonErrors.feedback: Root and power are right, but the fraction was never turned over for the minus sign.
The fraction was turned over, but the root and the power are still to come.

parts.stem:
$A = 9^{-\frac{3}{2}}$ and $B = 144^{-\frac{1}{2}} \times 2^{-1}$.

Which is larger, $A$ or $B$? You must show your working.

accepted: B is larger: A = 1/27 and B = 1/24
B is larger because A = 1/27 and B = 1/12 x 1/2 = 1/24

scheme.for: B identified as the larger, with the two values compared

hints: Write each as one over a whole number.
With 1 on top, the smaller bottom gives the larger number.
parts.workedSolution: $A = \dfrac{1}{9^{\frac{3}{2}}}$, and $\sqrt{9} = 3$, $3^{3} = 27$, so $A = \dfrac{1}{27}$. $B = \dfrac{1}{12} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{24}$. Both have 1 on top and 24 is less than 27, so $B$ is the larger.

commonErrors.feedback: Compared as 27 and 24 the order flips: the values are $\tfrac{1}{27}$ and $\tfrac{1}{24}$, and $\tfrac{1}{24}$ is the larger.

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh was asked to work out the value of $16^{\frac{3}{4}}$ without a calculator. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: On line 2 the index has been treated as a multiplier: $16$ was multiplied by $\dfrac{3}{4}$. An index is an instruction about powers and roots, so the $4$ underneath asks for a fourth root and the $3$ on top asks for a cube.
findTheMistake.feedback: Nothing here is careless: the arithmetic is fine, and the same slip appears every series. What is missing is the meaning of the index. Read $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$ as two jobs before you write anything: root by the bottom number, power by the top. Then the fourth root of $16$ is 2, and cubing it gives 8. If you are unsure whether a root is right, check it forwards: $2^{4} = 16$.

findTheMistake.stem: Ruairí was asked to work out the value of $8^{-\frac{2}{3}}$, giving his answer as a fraction. His working:
studentWorking: the index is negative, so the answer is -4
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: The root and the power on lines 1 and 2 are both correct and would earn the method mark. Line 3 reads the minus sign as a sign on the answer. A negative index means a reciprocal: $8^{-\frac{2}{3}} = \dfrac{1}{8^{\frac{2}{3}}}$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The method mark is safe, because the cube root and the square are exactly what the scheme wants to see. Only the last line costs you. The rule comes from $a^{n} \times a^{-n} = a^{0} = 1$: two numbers whose product is $1$ are reciprocals, so a negative index can never produce a negative answer from a positive base. Write the reciprocal line first, before any arithmetic, and the sign has nowhere to go wrong.

findTheMistake.stem: A candidate was asked to show that $81^{-\frac{3}{4}} = 1/27$. Their working:
studentWorking: 1/81 is not 1/27, so the statement is false
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right. On line 3 the $4$ has been used twice: once as the root, which was correct, and again as the power. The top number, $3$, is the power, so it should be $3^{3}$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The reciprocal line and the fourth root are both worth having, and they carry the method mark. The habit that prevents the rest is to write the two numbers down separately before you use either of them: bottom is the root, top is the power. It also pays to distrust a show-that answer that comes out false. On this paper a printed result is almost always true, so a mismatch is a signal to re-read your own working rather than to write a conclusion.

prompts.answer: The nth root of a: the number whose nth power is a.

prompts.prompt: In $a^{\frac{m}{n}}$, which number is the root?
prompts.answer: The bottom number, n, is the root; the top number, m, is the power.

prompts.prompt: What does a negative index mean?
prompts.answer: Take the reciprocal: $a^{-n}$ is one over $a^{n}$.
It is 1, because a power divided by itself is 1.

prompts.prompt: In what order do you do the jobs of $a^{-\frac{m}{n}}$?
prompts.answer: Turn it over, then take the root, then raise to the power.

prompts.prompt: Can a negative index make a positive base's answer negative?
prompts.answer: No: it gives a reciprocal, which is still positive.

prompts.prompt: What does a negative index do to a fraction base?
prompts.answer: It turns the fraction upside down, and the index becomes positive.

prompts.prompt: Where does the zero index in $5 \times 11^{0}$ apply?
prompts.answer: Only to the 11, so the value is 5.

findings.asked: Three short index values in one question: a zero index, an index of minus one and an index of minus three.
findings.wentWrong: The report describes this question as differentiating by ability: most of the entry handled the zero index, many handled the index of minus one, and only the stronger candidates handled the index of minus three.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the reciprocal line first for each negative index, so the minus sign was dealt with before any arithmetic began.
findings.rule: A negative index means one over the positive power. Write that line down before you work anything out.

findings.asked: An index simplification and a short numerical index proof in the same question.
findings.wentWrong: On the proof, fewer than half the entry built an argument the examiners were willing to accept, and more than half showed no grasp of what the two numbers in the index were there to do.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Split the fractional index into its two jobs on the page: the number underneath as the root, the number on top as the power, each on its own line.
findings.rule: In a show-that question the marks are on the chain of steps, so write the root and the power as separate lines.

findings.asked: A single index simplification carrying three marks.
findings.wentWrong: Examiners called the response very mixed, and the slips were of many different kinds: roughly a quarter of the entry took every mark and roughly a quarter took none.
findings.rule: Do one index job per line. Mixed errors come from trying to do the root, the power and the sign in a single step.

findings.asked: Four short index values, including a zero index on a term with a number in front of it.
findings.wentWrong: The report lists the commonest wrong answer part by part: 3 or 0 for the zero index, minus eight for one part, minus one thousand or minus thirty for 10 to the minus 3, and an answer that still contained the letter for the last part.
findings.rule: A zero index applies only to the symbol it sits on, and a minus index turns a power over rather than making it negative.

insight.ruleToRemember: Read the index before you touch the base: the minus sign means turn it over, the bottom number is the root, the top number is the power. Three small jobs, in that order, each on its own line.
insight.aStarSignal: Handling a negative fractional index on a fractional base in one clean chain, and being able to compare two such values without evaluating them as decimals.
